claim: Offset responses in auditory processing appear after a sound terminates.
source: Offset responses in auditory processing appear after a sound terminates.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about offset responses that is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Offset responses arise in neuronal circuits within the peripheral auditory system.
source: They arise in neuronal circuits within the peripheral auditory system, but their role in the central auditory system remains unknown.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: The role of offset responses in the central auditory system remains unknown.
source: They arise in neuronal circuits within the peripheral auditory system, but their role in the central auditory system remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Experimentally minimizing auditory cortical offset responses decreases mouse performance to detect sound termination.
source: At the perceptual level, our results reveal that experimentally minimizing auditory cortical offset responses decreases the mouse performance to detect sound termination, assigning a behavioral role to offset responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by behavioral experiments with optogenetic manipulation shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Cortical offset responses are not only inherited from the periphery but also amplified and generated de novo.
source: By combining in vivo electrophysiology in the auditory cortex and thalamus of awake mice, we also demonstrate that cortical offset responses are not only inherited from the periphery but also amplified and generated de novo.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological recordings comparing MGB and AAF responses shown in Figures 4-7.

claim: Offset responses code more than silence, including relevant changes in sound trajectories.
source: Finally, we show that offset responses code more than silence, including relevant changes in sound trajectories.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experiments with multifrequency component sounds shown in Figure 8.

claim: Cortical offset responses are important in encoding sound termination and detecting changes within temporally discontinuous sounds crucial for speech and vocalization.
source: Together, our results reveal the importance of cortical offset responses in encoding sound termination and detecting changes within temporally discontinuous sounds crucial for speech and vocalization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and their implications.

claim: Offset-responsive neurons are present in the cochlear nucleus.
source: Offset-responsive neurons are present through the whole auditory pathway starting from the cochlear nucleus (CN; Ding et al., 1999; Suga, 1964; Young and Brownell, 1976)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Offset-responsive neurons are present in the superior paraolivary nucleus.
source: to the superior paraolivary nucleus (SPN; Dehmel et al., 2002; Kulesza et al., 2003)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Offset-responsive neurons are present in the inferior colliculus.
source: the inferior colliculus (IC; Akimov et al., 2017; Kasai et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Offset-responsive neurons are present in the medial geniculate body.
source: the medial geniculate body (MGB; Anderson and Linden, 2016; He, 2001; He, 2002; Yu et al., 2004)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Offset-responsive neurons are present in the auditory cortex.
source: and the auditory cortex (ACx; Qin et al., 2007; Recanzone, 2000; Scholl et al., 2010; Takahashi et al., 2004)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Multiple mechanisms have been proposed to produce offset responses.
source: Multiple mechanisms have been proposed to produce offset responses (Bondanelli et al., 2019; Bondanelli et al., 2021; Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Signals from the cochlea can generate offset responses in the cochlear nucleus.
source: Generally, it is thought that signals from the cochlea can generate offset responses in both the CN (Suga, 1964) and the SPN (Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Signals from the cochlea can generate offset responses in the superior paraolivary nucleus.
source: Generally, it is thought that signals from the cochlea can generate offset responses in both the CN (Suga, 1964) and the SPN (Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Strong offset responses have mainly been described in the superior paraolivary nucleus.
source: but strong offset responses have mainly been described in the SPN.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: The superior paraolivary nucleus is considered specialized for offset response generation based on the strong inhibitory signal it receives during the sound and on the precise firing when the sound ends.
source: This structure is considered specialized for offset response generation based on the strong inhibitory signal it receives during the sound and on the precise firing when the sound ends.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: The superior paraolivary nucleus sends strong inhibitory inputs to the inferior colliculus.
source: The SPN sends then strong inhibitory inputs to the IC (Kulesza and Berrebi, 2000; Saldaña et al., 2009)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The inferior colliculus might convey offset response signals to the medial geniculate body.
source: which might further convey the signal to MGB.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the pathway of offset response signals.

claim: Offset responses in MGB and ACx are generally thought to be driven by excitatory/inhibitory inputs from IC rather than by other neural mechanisms.
source: Offset responses in MGB and the ACx are generally thought to be driven by excitatory/inhibitory inputs from IC rather than by other neural mechanisms (Kopp-Scheinpflug et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Bondanelli et al. argued for a role of recurrent A1 connectivity in shaping offset responses in cortex.
source: Recently, Bondanelli et al. argued for a role of recurrent A1 connectivity in shaping offset responses in cortex, and suggested that cortical offset responses could be generated at a higher level of recurrency (Bondanelli et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Bondanelli et al. suggested that cortical offset responses could be generated at a higher level of recurrency.

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: De novo generation or amplification of offset responses in MGB and ACx have not been demonstrated experimentally yet.
source: However, de novo generation or amplification of offset responses in MGB and ACx have not been demonstrated experimentally yet (Bondanelli et al., 2019; He, 2003; Kasai et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2004).

claim: The perceptual significance of offset responses has been difficult to assess.
source: The perceptual significance of offset responses has been difficult to assess.

claim: Offset responses are generally weaker and slower than onset responses.

claim: Offset responses have been observed in twice as many cells in AAF as in A1.
source: At the cortical level, offset responses have been shown to cluster within the anterior auditory field (AAF) – a primary region of the ACx – where they have been observed in twice as many cells as in the primary auditory cortex (A1) (Sołyga and Barkat, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Offset responses are highly influenced by different sound parameters.
source: Offset responses are also highly influenced by different sound parameters.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: AAF is highly specialized for processing information on sound termination.
source: Our results reveal that AAF is highly specialized for processing information on sound termination and that minimizing its offset responses decreases the mouse performance to detect when a sound ends.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the data showing high proportion of onset-offset cells in AAF (Figure 4) and behavioral experiments (Figures 1-2).

claim: Minimizing AAF offset responses decreases the mouse performance to detect when a sound ends.
source: Our results reveal that AAF is highly specialized for processing information on sound termination and that minimizing its offset responses decreases the mouse performance to detect when a sound ends.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by behavioral experiments with optogenetic manipulation shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: AAF, unlike MGB, shows a significant increase in offset response amplitudes with sound duration.
source: First, we found that AAF, unlike MGB, shows a significant increase in offset response amplitudes with sound duration.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6.

claim: White noise bursts only evoke offset responses in AAF but not in MGB.
source: Then, we report that white noise (WN) bursts – unlike pure tones – only evoke offset responses in AAF but not in MGB.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7.

claim: Offset responses are present in AAF whenever a frequency component is removed from multifrequency stimuli.
source: Finally, we show that offset responses are present in AAF whenever a frequency component is removed from multifrequency stimuli and therefore may have a further role than solely coding silence.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experiments with multifrequency component sounds shown in Figure 8.

claim: Offset responses may have a further role than solely coding silence.
source: Finally, we show that offset responses are present in AAF whenever a frequency component is removed from multifrequency stimuli and therefore may have a further role than solely coding silence.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings with multifrequency stimuli.

claim: AAF offset responses are involved in tracking sound duration.
source: Taken together, our findings suggest a particular involvement of AAF offset responses in sound termination processing and point to the importance of this cortical subfield for advanced processing such as tracking sound duration or detecting changes in frequency and level within temporally discontinuous sounds.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing duration-dependent offset responses in AAF.

claim: AAF offset responses are involved in detecting changes in frequency and level within temporally discontinuous sounds.
source: Taken together, our findings suggest a particular involvement of AAF offset responses in sound termination processing and point to the importance of this cortical subfield for advanced processing such as tracking sound duration or detecting changes in frequency and level within temporally discontinuous sounds.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings with multifrequency stimuli.

claim: Transient offset responses cluster within AAF rather than A1.
source: As, at the cortical level, transient offset responses cluster within AAF rather than A1 (Sołyga and Barkat, 2019)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Offset responses are absent in the averaged population activity of A1 neurons in response to 9 kHz PT in awake preparations.
source: and are absent in the averaged population activity of A1 neurons in response to 9 kHz PT in awake preparations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)

claim: Mice were trained to detect the end of 9 kHz pure tones.
source: we developed a sound termination detection task in which mice expressing channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) in parvalbumin-positive (PV+) cells learned to detect the end of 9 kHz pure tones (PT; Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the behavioral task.

claim: The duration of the tones was varied randomly (1, 1.5, or 2 s) to avoid a putative expected behavioral response at a fixed delay after sound onset.
source: The duration of the tones was varied randomly (1, 1.5, or 2 s) to avoid a putative expected behavioral response at a fixed delay after sound onset.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the experimental design.

claim: Mice were initially trained with a tone played at 80 dB SPL.
source: Mice were initially trained with a tone played at 80 dB SPL (sound pressure level) (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: A reaction time window was set to 3 s during initial training sessions and progressively shortened to 1 s in the final training sessions.
source: A reaction time window was set to 3 s during initial training sessions and progressively shortened to 1 s in the final training sessions.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: An increase in correct offset detection (hit rate) reflected successful learning.
source: An increase in correct offset detection (hit rate), a decrease in reaction time over the training sessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), and a significant difference between hit rate and licks at the chance level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e–g) reflected successful learning after which animals were moved to the test phase (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the criteria for successful learning in the behavioral task.

claim: A decrease in reaction time over the training sessions reflected successful learning.
source: An increase in correct offset detection (hit rate), a decrease in reaction time over the training sessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), and a significant difference between hit rate and licks at the chance level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e–g) reflected successful learning after which animals were moved to the test phase (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the criteria for successful learning in the behavioral task.

claim: A significant difference between hit rate and licks at the chance level reflected successful learning.
source: An increase in correct offset detection (hit rate), a decrease in reaction time over the training sessions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), and a significant difference between hit rate and licks at the chance level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e–g) reflected successful learning after which animals were moved to the test phase (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the criteria for successful learning in the behavioral task.

claim: Laser light (473 nm) was delivered above AAF for 200 ms starting at sound termination to activate PV+ cells and reduce offset responses in non-PV+ cells.
source: In half of the trials (pseudorandomized each day), a laser light (473 nm) was delivered above AAF for 200 ms starting at sound termination (Figure 1e) to activate PV+ cells (Figure 1f) and to significantly reduce offset responses in non-PV+ cells (Figure 1f).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation and its effects shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Preventing AAF offset responses significantly decreased the performance to detect sound termination (Δ ODI (off–on) = 0.23 ± 0.06).
source: Comparing the animals' performance during laser-on and laser-off trials showed that preventing AAF offset responses significantly decreased the performance to detect sound termination (Figure 1g, h, Δ ODI (off–on) = 0.23 ± 0.06).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1g, h.

claim: Reaction times were significantly longer in laser-on compared to laser-off trials.
source: Interestingly, reaction times were significantly longer in laser-on compared to laser-off trials (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The laser alone had no effect on neural activity in wild-type animals.
source: The laser alone had no effect, neither at the neural (Figure 1j) nor at the behavior level (Figure 1k,l, Δ ODI (off–on) = 0.15 ± 0.11).
evidence: This is a control experiment result shown in Figure 1j, k, l.

claim: The laser alone had no effect on behavioral performance in wild-type animals (Δ ODI (off–on) = 0.15 ± 0.11).

claim: Laser presentation during the ongoing sound did not result in any significant change in the animals' performance (Δ ODI (off–on) = −0.02 ± 0.12).

claim: Offset responses in AAF are behaviorally relevant in the sound termination detection task.

claim: Previous studies illustrated how offset responses in the ACx of rats and cats strongly depend on the fall-time of a sound.
source: Previous studies illustrated how offset responses in the ACx of rats and cats strongly depend on the fall-time of a sound (Qin et al., 2007; Takahashi et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fast fall-ramps (0.01 ms) lead to significantly higher offset responses than longer ones (10.0 ms).
source: As expected from previous studies, fast fall-ramps (0.01 ms) lead to significantly higher offset responses than longer ones (10.0 ms), as tested during awake passive recordings (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) or when animals were performing a behavioral task (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a finding supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2a, b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sounds with a 0.01 ms fall-ramp are not causing an additional artificial onset response.
source: We confirmed that the sounds with a 0.01 ms fall-ramp are not causing an additional artificial onset response (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a control experiment result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: For the fast fall-ramp, a weak spectral splatter was detected present for less than 0.5 ms and covering the frequency range between 6 and 30 kHz.
source: For the fast fall-ramp, we detected a weak spectral splatter present for less than 0.5 ms and covering the frequency range between 6 and 30 kHz (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c, d).
evidence: This is a finding from acoustic measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c, d.

claim: Neurons with a best frequency within the spectral splatter frequency range did not display a more significant response to sound termination.
source: We did not observe any increased offset response in those neurons compared to neurons with other BF (Figure 2—figure supplement 2e), indicating that putative onset responses to the splatter could not be significant.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2e.

claim: The offset responses to fast and slow ramps correlated highly (ρ = 0.71, p < 0.0001).
source: We showed that the offset responses to fast and slow ramps correlated highly (Figure 2—figure supplement 2f, ρ = 0.71, p < 0.0001, Spearman correlation), suggesting that our protocol allows us to identify actual offset responses.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2f.

claim: Onset responses were suppressed by preceding onset responses but not affected by preceding offset responses.
source: We found that onset responses were suppressed by preceding onset responses but not affected by preceding offset responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 2g), even when the interval was as short as 50 ms.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2g.

claim: Offset responses are driven by different synapses than onset responses.
source: This suggests that the offset responses we recorded are driven by different synapses that onset responses and cannot be onset responses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and previous knowledge.

claim: Mice could correctly detect when sounds ended for tones with both short and long ramps.

claim: MGB cells projecting to AAF were clustered mainly as onset–offset cells (82%).

claim: Some sustained (9%) and onset (9%) cells projecting from MGB to AAF were identified, but their representation was significantly lower.

claim: Offset responses in AAF are mainly inherited from MGB.

claim: The increase in offset response amplitude with sound duration is not unique to one layer in AAF.

claim: MGB does not contain fast-spiking interneurons.

claim: A significant correlation between offset spike rate and sound duration was found in both FS and RS neurons in AAF.

claim: One cell population alone is not driving the dependence of offset responses on sound duration in AAF.

claim: There is a clear amplification of the dependence of offset responses on sound duration in AAF as compared to MGB.

claim: In MGB, 500 ms WN evoked no offset responses above spontaneous activity, unlike PT of the same length.
